    AI Overview
    Genocide is defined under international law as specific acts—including killing, causing harm, creating destructive conditions, preventing births, and transferring children—committed with the
    intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944, it is considered the "crime of crimes". 
    Legal Definition and Components 
    The 1948 UN Convention defines genocide by specific acts committed with this intent, covering both public officials and private individuals. Key legal elements include: 
    • Intent: Specific intent (dolus specialis) to destroy the group as such.
    • Targeted Groups: Protection applies to national, ethnical, racial, or religious groups.
    • Accountability: Punishes conspiracy, incitement, attempt, and complicity. 
    Historical Examples 
    Significant historical instances include the Armenian Genocide (1915–1923), the Holocaust (1941–1945), the Cambodian Genocide (1970s), the Rwandan Genocide (1994), and the Srebrenica Massacre (1995). 
    Contemporary Concerns and Situations 
    Recent reports and investigations have highlighted potential or alleged genocides in several regions: 
    • Rohingya (Myanmar): Legal action against leaders for actions against the Rohingya.
    • Gaza (Palestine): Allegations and reports from UN bodies regarding actions in Gaza.
    • Sudan: Reports indicating potential genocide by the RSF. 
    Genocide vs. Other Crimes 
    While often confused with other atrocities, genocide has a distinct legal definition compared to war crimes, crimes against humanity, and ethnic cleansing. 
    Stages of Genocide 
    Researcher Gregory Stanton identified ten stages, including Classification, Dehumanization, Polarization, and Denial, which are often used to identify and understand the process of genocide.

    What is the legal definition of genocide intent?
    To constitute genocide, there must be a proven intent on the part of perpetrators to physically destroy a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Cultural destruction does not suffice, nor does an intention to simply disperse a group.

    Genocide is the partial or total destruction of a human group, committed intentionally. The popular view conceives of genocide as the large-scale killing of individuals, but in the scholarly and legal fields, genocide occurs when the group itself is targeted.
    Source: Wikipedia
